oil.summary: Crude benchmarks edged higher Monday as Hormuz disruption fears remained front and centre. Brent added 0.70% to $89.15 and WTI rose 0.51% to $82.84, extending modest weekly and monthly gains. Tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz slowed further over the weekend, three vessels were reported damaged amid the US-Iran conflict, and Washington is preparing fresh Iran sanctions following stalled talks. Asian refiners are already rerouting Saudi cargoes via Egypt to avoid Red Sea risk. China provided partial demand support, with July imports jumping 22% year-on-year and the country adding an estimated 200,000 bpd to strategic reserves. Oil majors are reported to have reaped a $93 billion windfall from the crisis. The sharp outlier was RBOB gasoline, off nearly 9% on the day and down over 14% on the month — the data provided no explanatory headline for that move.
drivers: Strait of Hormuz near-closure sustaining supply-risk premium in crude benchmarks
China strategic reserve build and 22% import surge providing demand-side support
US preparing new Iran sanctions; Israeli strikes in Lebanon keeping geopolitical risk elevated

gas.summary: Henry Hub slid 1.54% to $2.689/MMBtu, extending a steep monthly decline of 7.56%, while European TTF moved in the opposite direction, gaining 0.83% to €61.935/MWh and up nearly 8% over the past month. The transatlantic divergence reflects a deepening European storage crunch reported ahead of the heating season, with inventories described as increasingly pressing with fewer than three months to go. On the US side, Trump has publicly told Americans to accept higher gas prices, though domestic spot prices are falling rather than rising. India's ONGC secured a US OFAC licence to return to Venezuelan operations, a development that could incrementally ease global supply tightness. Headline coverage for this sector was relatively thin today.
drivers: European gas storage shortfall tightening TTF ahead of heating season
Henry Hub in persistent retreat, down over 7% on the month, reflecting loose US domestic balances
India's ONGC Venezuela licence re-entry could add incremental non-Middle East supply

power.summary: EU carbon EUAs edged down 0.61% to $77.34, a modest pullback within a broader month-to-date gain of 2.77%, likely tracking the modest softening in risk appetite rather than any fundamental shift. The primary macro shadow over the power sector remains rising gas costs via TTF, up 8% over the month, which squeezes gas-fired generation margins and theoretically supports carbon prices through fuel-switching dynamics. On structural themes, a report highlighted that just 7% of US nuclear fuel is domestically sourced, complicating the administration's nuclear renaissance push. India offered delayed solar developers a fee-based option to retain grid connectivity rather than forfeit it, signalling regulatory flexibility to keep renewable pipelines moving. Ukraine's deep-strike operations against Russian energy infrastructure were also noted. Dedicated power-price data beyond EUAs and TTF was not available today.
drivers: Rising TTF squeezing gas-fired generation margins and providing underlying EUA support
US nuclear fuel import dependency flagged as structural constraint on domestic nuclear expansion
India's grid-access relief for delayed solar projects supports renewable build-out momentum
